In the first half of the eighteenth century some of Rameau's works use the piccolo; the Paris Opera orchestra had an octave transverse flute by 1735 at the latest. Only around 1800 did the piccolo gain a stable place in the orchestra. Small flute names in Baroque scores mostly mean a small recorder, and Vivaldi's concertos for the instrument belong to that group. Until the end of the nineteenth century the piccolo kept the simple-system construction of the Baroque, Classical and Romantic periods; at the end of the century it began to adopt the Boehm mechanism, which became standard in the twentieth century, though the body kept a slight taper and its lowest note is D.

Its high register has a metallic sheen, and the sound is light and agile, full of energy. As the highest instrument of the flute family, the piccolo sounds an octave above the ordinary flute, its range concentrated in the high frequencies, which makes it especially suited to fast, brilliant passages. Its resonating cavity is small, the resonant space is limited, and the sound it produces is relatively clean and simple. Compared with the trumpet, its timbre is brighter and more delicate; compared with the soprano saxophone it lacks warmth and sounds sharper. The piccolo is often used to heighten a joyful, light or dramatic mood in a piece.

The piccolo is a European aerophone of the woodwind family, a variant of the flute family of Western music, classified H-S 421.121.12-71. It is smaller than the ordinary flute, about half its length, has the same fingering as the transverse flute and sounds an octave higher. In construction the headjoint is mostly cylindrical and the body slightly conical, the keys are smaller, and it is blown with an embouchure. The modern piccolo is used in symphony orchestras, marching bands and wind ensembles, often in unison with the flute or the violin, and is also played by the third flautist; in the traditional Basel Carnival formations it is used together with the marching drum.
